item.title: Emacs vs Neovim - Why the Emacs Community Is So Nice (Sacha Chua)
item.description:
youtube

🔴 Watch Neovim + kitty Maintainers on AI, Terminal Security and What's Next | Justin M. Keyes & Kovid Goyal (live Nov 8): https://youtube.com/live/C0kQDam7PZs I asked Sacha Chua why the Emacs subreddit feels like rainbows and butterflies while the Neovim one can get so heated. Is it older users, or does your editor make you grumpy? Her answer is about sharing: Emacs customizations are personal tools you hand to others as a gift, with no guarantee they will work for anyone else, and that habit has built a community around blog posts, literate configs and looking over each other's shoulders. From there we talk about what the Neovim community could borrow. I bring up Dotfyle and why a human curator matters, and Sacha explains how she puts Emacs News together in an hour or two with a lot of automation. She also shares advice for newcomers: go connect with people through meetups, Reddit, IRC and mailing lists, and don't try to learn Emacs alone. The conversation ends on the idea that it's not Neovim versus Emacs. We cover how ideas and workflows cross over between editors, how EmacsConf runs as a free online conference, and why org.nvim could be a friendly entry point for Neovim users curious about Org Mode. item.title: Emacs for Everything - Why Sacha Chua Still Lives in Emacs After 20+ Years
item.description:
youtube

In this episode I sit down with Sacha Chua @sachactube, who has been living in Emacs for more than 20 years and shares the Emacs world through Emacs News, Emacs Chat and EmacsConf. She demos the workflows she has built one small hack at a time: real-time speech recognition transcripts inside Emacs, local CPU-only dictation on a 2018 laptop, voice commands that control OBS (because "start streaming" sometimes comes out as "start screaming"), editing video by reordering subtitle cues, generating title cards from WebVTT with ImageMagick, and turning video transcripts into searchable blog posts with chapters and screenshots. She also explains why for her Linux is just the library Emacs uses to talk to the hardware, why she stays on XFCE and X11, how Emacspeak helped when her laptop screen failed, and how she captures tasks from her phone with Orgzly Revived and Syncthing. We also get into the bigger questions. Sacha shares how she uses LLMs in a limited way she can understand, why she plans to sit out the AI churn, how AI-generated code connects to The Lisp Curse, how maintainers can deal with AI slop patches, and whether editors and terminals still matter when people go fully agentic. Of course I had to bring up Neovim: why there is no NeovimConf anymore, why the Neovim subreddit feels toxic while the Emacs community is so friendly, what Neovim could learn from Planet Emacs Life and Emacs News, and a planned Emacs and Neovim panel with Prot. If you are an Emacs beginner, a Neovim user curious about the other side, or just into plain text, automation and speech tools, Sacha's advice to connect with people and her many small automations are worth hearing. item.title: Emacs Voice Control With Local AI on a 2018 Laptop - Sacha Chua's Setup
item.description:
youtube

I ask Sacha Chua @sachactube how her speech to text works in real time, and the answer surprised me: it's an entirely local model running on CPU only, on a Lenovo P52 from around 2018. She uses a Parakeet-based multilingual model behind an OpenAI-style server that plugs straight into her Emacs setup, and it handles both her English and her French. From there we get into what dictation unlocks in Emacs. Sacha shows voice commands that start and stop her OBS stream (because "start streaming" kept turning into "start screaming"), a laser-cursor mode, and a Ctrl+semicolon substitution that fixes a misrecognized word everywhere and remembers the correction for next time. I compare it with my own setup, where I transcribe locally on my Mac and struggle with words like Neovim. She also walks through how a live transcript grew out of small hacks, how she talks to Emacs (including a French practice conversation using gptel and Gemini), and how Org Mode helps her capture tasks in tiny chunks of time as a parent. If you want voice control, better transcripts, or a calmer capture workflow, there are plenty of ideas here to borrow, even if you stay in Neovim like me. item.title: Supertag 0.4 for Emacs: one sentence, one interface for each kind of Org note
item.description:
youtube

Supertag 0.4 gives each kind of Org note its own interface. Describe in one sentence how a tag's stream should work, and a model writes a Stream agent for it: groups, a line per note, and keys that fill in properties. After that the agent runs without the model, and you can revise it one sentence at a time as your needs change. Everything stays in plain Org text. Agents never create notes; a key press writes an ordinary property, SCHEDULED or DEADLINE line. Delete an agent and your notes are untouched. Chapters 0:00 One stream of everything 0:45 One line to find: words, tag:, KEY:VALUE, (query) 1:40 Discovery: search by meaning 2:15 A Stream agent from one sentence (contacts) 3:30 Projects: dates and tasks under their project 4:46 A reading log for #book 6:24 It grows with you: revise, code, manage 7:50 Archived notes step aside 8:25 A whole file is a node 9:05 Upgrade Notes on the recording - A real Emacs session on a made-up demo vault; every key press is real. - The agents are written live by DeepSeek (deepseek-v4-flash) through gptel. The waits for the model are sped up, with a label giving the real time. - Discovery's meaning search uses bge-m3 through Ollama; it is optional. ,#Emacs #OrgMode #PKM

item.title: What kind of AI interaction do we actually need? Get ideas from Lifestreams
item.description:
youtube

What kind of interaction with AI do we actually need? An AI agent gets small edits right most of the time, but only most of the time, so you end up checking its work almost every time. This video looks at a different approach: let the AI write an interface once, then use that interface every day without calling the model again. The idea goes back to Lifestreams, a 1997 research prototype from Yale. It had no folders and no file names. Everything lived in one time-ordered stream, and two kinds of processors worked on top of it: Summarize, which decided how a stream is shown, and Agents, which decided what you can do with it. The idea never caught on because someone had to write those processors by hand. Supertag brings that idea to plain Org files in Emacs. You describe what you want in one sentence, and a model writes an agent for that kind of note, such as contacts grouped by how close you are, with a key that logs today's date. After that the agent runs on its own, with no model involved. A second processor, Summary, draws a live overview of a stream. Three rules keep it honest: 1. The text is the only truth. Delete the agent and every note is still there. 2. The model runs only when you ask, to design an agent or to revise one. 3. Every interface is built from trusted parts and checked before it is installed. Chapters 0:00 What kind of AI interaction do we need? 0:22 One key, built once 0:40 Lifestreams, 1997: one stream, two processors 1:13 The missing piece was the author 1:44 Supertag: one sentence makes a contacts interface 2:19 Projects, and revising an agent 2:38 Summary: a live overview 2:49 Three rules 3:17 An AI layer, behind everything Credits Lifestreams figures: Eric Freeman, "The Lifestreams Software Architecture", PhD dissertation, Yale University, 1997. Shown for commentary. Demo: a made-up English demo vault running in Emacs; no real personal data. Narration: synthetic voice (Qwen3-TTS). Music: original, generated locally with MusicGen. ,#Emacs #OrgMode #AI

item.title: Emacs vs Neovim - Why Prot Won't Pick a Side
item.description:
youtube

After all my Neovim talk, Rumen brought @protesilaos (Prot) onto Root Access to balance things out, and Ted joined us too. Rumen shares that he converted to Emacs full time, is building a NixOS flavor, runs his tasks in Org mode, and is working on a small database server so the notes he dictates on his phone sync to Emacs on his desktop and laptop. We also get into the anti-AI "Human Emacs" fork idea, and Prot explains why Emacs already refuses LLM-generated contributions over copyright and GPL licensing concerns, and how maintainers spot suspicious patches. Prot says he doesn't use AI because programming is basically his video game, but he admits the technology case is undeniable and frames the AI bubble as a capital realignment like the dot-com crash. We also talk about how Cyprus and Greece export tourism and land, and the gold rush mentality that comes with it, and I ask Prot about Cypriot olive oil for my wife. Then it's Niri and scrolling window managers versus i3/Sway-style control, Emacs workspaces replacing tmux, and DHH's Omarchy, where Prot argues software should be judged on its merits and not its author, and explains why he refuses to remove a Modus theme port for Omarchy. I show Hazenbug's org mode plugin for Neovim, Prot explains why org is portable plain-text markup, and I explain why I'm not switching back to Emacs yet - I'm not on the Neovim team or the Emacs team, and editor choice shouldn't be treated like soccer or religion. If you care about Emacs, Neovim, free software, or how AI fits into all of it, this one is for you. item.title: Emacs and rust on an ASUS Eee PC 1000HA
item.description:
youtube

In an effort to focus/mood setting, I am using these random devices for specific purposes eg. I use a black 2007 Macbook Pro to journal in and I'm using this one to learn rust in. Netbook info: - ASUS Eee PC 1000HA - Using Debian 12 - i686 arch The battery is shot and hard to find a good one to replace it with. I have 3 bad batteries from my attempts to get a good one. The one I use in this video can hold a charge for like 10 minutes so it's helpful. Installing emacs and rust - $sudo apt install rust - $sudo apt install emacs See screen at 2:41 for modifications in init.el file. My install did not come with an init.el file so I had to make it under /home/user/.emacs.d/init.el. The .emacs.d file is made automatically. As you make edits through the Emacs GUI eg. with M-x command settings are written to the init.el file. That's how I was able to get the theme to stick and later when installing rust-mode package to get syntax highlighting to work. I primarily had to use the Emacs GUI to get the theme installed/other situations addressed like the rust syntax highlighting. For rust don't use the curl/bash script method to install it, just stick with apt and then you'll have to bind the /usr/bin/rustc command to rustc if you want it to be easier to type. item.title: Emacs vs Neovim - Why He Switched for Good
item.description:
youtube

🔴 LIVE Sun, Nov 8, 7:30 AM CST: Neovim + kitty Maintainers on AI, Terminal Security and What's Next | Justin M. Keyes & Kovid Goyal. Set a reminder: https://youtube.com/live/C0kQDam7PZs Why would someone leave Neovim for Emacs and stay there? In this clip, lucidlynx explains why everything in Neovim felt like a separate piece that never quite fit together, and why Emacs felt more integrated. I jump in with my own experience: I tried Emacs, I suffered, and I get what they mean about the Neovim ecosystem feeling like a puzzle of disconnected tools. We get into LunarVim disappearing, LazyVim's rapid-fire changes (like the move from nvim-cmp to blink.cmp breaking completion plugins), and how shell tools like EZA, BAT, ripgrep, FD, FZF and Zoxide never felt like part of a whole. lucidlynx also shares what the switch was actually like: remapping Caps Lock to Control, getting used to Emacs keybindings, and starting out with Doom Emacs. Later we talk about Emacs as a Lisp machine, using AI to port a VS Code plugin for HashiCorp Packer into Emacs, and why Org mode keeps coming up. If you're curious about Emacs, or tired of stitching your Neovim setup together, this one is worth a watch. item.title: grid-table — Runs Excel in Emacs
item.description:
youtube

grid-table (now rename to exc.el) is a spreadsheet for Emacs that behaves like Excel: the keys, the formulas, the error values and the file format. This tour uses one workbook, Northwind Tea Co., about 2,400 orders on three sheets, and shows what is new in 0.4. What you'll see: - The new view, drawn with ETAF, next to the old one - Excel keys: typing, RET, TAB, F2, fill, copy and paste with formats, undo - XLOOKUP, SUMIFS, FILTER, dynamic arrays that spill, LET and LAMBDA - One edit recalculates only what depends on it - Tracing where a number comes from, with error values that behave like Excel's - Floating charts over the cells - Results checked against Microsoft's own function examples - Export to .xlsx, edit in LibreOffice, open it again in Emacs - A workbook that reads another workbook's values - A new formula function in three lines of Lisp - Inside Org notes, and in a terminal Chapters: 0:00 Old view and new view, same edit 0:38 grid-table 0:49 Excel keys 1:34 Clean the orders 2:10 Look up and summarise 3:19 One edit, and only what depends on it 4:51 Make it presentable 5:25 Where did this number come from? 6:33 Names 8:00 Arrays that spill 9:50 LAMBDA 10:59 Text, dates and R1C1 13:15 A chart that floats 14:56 Checked against Excel 15:33 Send it to a colleague (.xlsx) 16:36 A workbook that reads another 17:36 Three lines of Lisp 18:08 In Org notes and in a terminal 18:32 Get it
